slides.say: A lock code has three digits, and each digit is one, three or five. A digit may repeat. Which of the following cannot be the product of the three digits?

So we build a product out of three digits, and every digit is one, three or five. The question is which number can't be built, and that's really a question about a missing prime. [short pause] We'll solve it two ways, breaking each choice into primes, and then even and odd.
at: every digit is one, three or five

slides.say: [short pause] Our first method. What primes can the digits bring? One brings nothing, it doesn't change a product. Three brings a three, and five brings a five. So any product we build has only threes and fives in it, and at most three of them, because there are three digits.
Forty-five. Forty-five is nine times five, and nine is three times three. So three, three, five. Exactly three digits, the code three, three, five. It works, so choice number one is out.
Thirty. Thirty is two times fifteen, so two times three times five. It needs a two. Can any digit bring a two? One, three, five, no. So thirty can't be built.

In the exam you'd circle it and move on. Here, let's check the rest. Twenty-five is five times five. The code needs three digits, so use one for the third digit. Multiplying by one does not change twenty-five. The code is one, five, five, so choice number three is out.
Fifteen is three times five, and again a one for the third digit, one, three, five. Choice number four is out. So thirty, choice number two is our answer.
at: choice number two is our answer

slides.say: [pause] All the digits are odd. And odd times odd is always odd. Three times five is fifteen, and five times five is twenty-five, odd every time. Why? An even product needs a factor of two somewhere, and odd numbers don't have a two in them.
at: odd times odd is always odd

slides.say: So a product of three odd digits is always odd. Thirty is even, so it can't be the product. Choice number two. [pause] Okay. I'll see you in the next question.
